General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1499 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits.
  • Industry observers note that researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
  • Sources indicate that the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Industry observers note that researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

Sources indicate that the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the upcoming findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk.

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

In a recent development, people consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Industry observers note that moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

In a recent development, the contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk.".

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

In a recent development, wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health.

It has been revealed that to make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Recent findings suggest that alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Industry observers note that nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an vital distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the upcoming. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

It has been revealed that A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the upcoming house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:.

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:.

It has been revealed that greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert indicates, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the fresh place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need.".

This is also a great time to move additional services to the fresh address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:.

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the newly introduced home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flying over the Arizona desert one day in 2023, Beau Phillips looked out his plane window and spotted thousands of shipping containers—remnants of a dismantled border wall—scattered across the arid landscape.

That chance glimpse sparked an idea: convert the abandoned steel boxes into hundreds of affordable housing units and build a whole new community in the Tucson area for some of the 40,000 low-income residents waiting for housing assistance.

Industry observers note that "These were built to keep people out, and now we're welcoming people in," Phillips tells Realtor.com®. "There is a poetic justice there.".

It has been revealed that phillips, a semiretired MTV Networks and radio marketing executive, first encountered the containers in late 2022, when he took part in a demonstration protesting then-Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey's order to install a border barrier made up of more than 2,000 double-stacked steel shipping crates, topped with wire, near Yuma and in the Coronado National Forest.

After the Biden administration and environmental groups successfully sued, arguing that the 10-mile wall of containers was illegally placed on federal and tribal land, the state took the barrier apart in early 2023.

Some 2,200 steel boxes were left in the desert with no plan for their disposal, until Phillips saw them from a plane and pitched state officials on a new use for them.

To bring his vision to life, Phillips founded a nonprofit, Boxes of Hope, and teamed up with La Frontera AZ, a major affordable housing developer and behavioral health provider, to create a village made up of 350 to 450 shipping containers transformed into rental homes.

This project is aimed at singles, couples, veterans, seniors, and anyone priced out of Tucson’s rental market, where the median asking rent in October was $1,133, according to the latest data from Realtor.com.

"We're really opening it up wide to just whoever needs it, and we will make sure that the rent that is charged is affordable," notes Phillips.

The proposed 25- to 30-acre community will take shape in Southeast Tucson, within 2 miles of the containers' current resting place to minimize transport costs. The site also sits along a bus line and within a half-mile of shopping.

Phillips, who freely admits that he knows "nothing about swinging a hammer," tapped Tucson native Ryan Egan, a veteran container-conversion expert, to lead construction on the ambitious building project, which is at the moment in the fundraising stage.

It takes about $59,000 to turn a 4-ton crate into a comfortable 300-square-foot residence insulated against Arizona's brutal 115-degree summers.

"It's about half the price that the city of Tucson now pays for-profit builders to build affordable housing, so they're thrilled," notes Phillips.

Each unit will be air-conditioned, with a private bedroom and queen bed, full bathroom, kitchenette with a refrigerator and a two-burner stovetop, storage, fresh flooring, windows, and sliding glass doors.

Sources indicate that "It would be almost like someone who lives in an RV park," explains the Boxes of Hope founder and CEO. "You have your unit that you live in, and you connect to utilities on site.".

The exteriors will be sandblasted and decorated with colorful murals celebrating Tucson's culture.

Beyond providing a roof and four walls, Phillips and his project partner, La Frontera CEO Dan Ranieri, envision a holistic neighborhood complete with a park, laundry facilities, a community kitchen and dining hall, behavioral healthcare, transitional housing for the homeless, and on-site training in building trades like carpentry and plumbing,.

"It's really a 360-degree solution to get people not just a place to live, but a place where they can thrive," notes Phillips.

In a recent development, boxes of Hope already has backing from Sen. Mark Kelly's office, the Arizona Department of Housing, and Tucson city leadership. The nonprofit is at the moment meeting with potential donors and pursuing government and private housing grants to move the project from planning into construction.

To any locals harboring "not in my backyard" concerns about the future affordable rental community, Phillips stresses that his team aims to be good neighbors from the start.

"We're going to meet with neighborhood groups. We're going to explain our vision," he states. " We want to listen to people, but we also want them to understand that we're trying to do something good here. We're trying to take lemons and turn them into lemonade.".

He points to La Frontera's track record of managing affordable housing, which includes the development of nearly a dozen low-income tax credit projects since 2008.

Boxes of Hope looks to unveil its full development proposal and the village's exact location site in January 2027, after signing a letter of intent with the landowner.

"He loves the concept so much that he dropped his price in half and said, 'I want to help you,'" Phillips recalls.

Industry observers note that despite the project's ambitious scope, the construction timeline moves rapidly. Turning a raw container into a finished home takes about two weeks, and once production ramps up, Phillips expects the team to complete 12 to 15 conversions per month.

Site development is set to get underway in spring 2027, with the first tenants poised to move in by the second half of next year.

Beyond Tucson, Phillips believes that Boxes of Hope could serve as a blueprint for tackling America's broader housing affordability crisis.

Industry observers note that " Last year, 25 million shipping containers arrived in the U.S. along the West Coast and never left because America doesn't export anywhere near as much as we import," he claims. "Most of them are still sitting all along the West Coast in Seattle and San Diego and San Francisco and Portland.".

According to recent reports, that need for well-priced rental inventory is felt acutely nationwide. According to the latest Realtor.com monthly rental report, the median asking rent in October rose year over year for the first time since 2023, driven by a sharp decline in multifamily construction,.

However, Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu points out that container conversions have inherent limitations.

"A container can be converted into a studio fairly easily, but it is hard to build larger units with multiple bedrooms that meet the needs of families," she says.

Healthcare growth and engagement solutions provider WebMD Ignite is bringing in OpenAI’s ChatGPT to support health systems in advertising.

It has been revealed that the latest offering will combine direct platform support with WebMD Ignite’s expertise in healthcare campaign strategy, creative, activation and measurement. It will allow clients to evaluate how ChatGPT advertising can support their own growth goals.

WebMD Ignite Healthcare Solutions Group President Ann Bilyew told Fierce Healthcare the increasing use of ChatGPT and other tools prior to care “changes where they [health systems] need to be visible.”.

WebMD Ignite has already begun activating campaigns, executives say, including one with a leading academic medical center involving cardiology. The initial campaign has tested creative variations, aligned messaging and more.

When it comes to protecting patient trust, Bilyew said ChatGPT labels advertisements and separates them from answers.

Recent findings suggest that “OpenAI also sets eligibility requirements for healthcare advertisers and excludes personal health conversations from ad placements,” she said. “At WebMD Ignite, we bring experience on both sides. We understand how people look for care and how health systems communicate about the services they offer. That shapes the words we choose, the claims we make and where someone lands after clicking an ad.”.

WebMD Ignite claims it works with more than 650 health systems—including 95% of the 150 largest in the U.S.—and 80% of the 20 largest payers.

Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering key questions about its effects on mental health.
  • Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • Industry observers note that the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering key questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

Industry observers note that the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

Industry observers note that "What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," mentioned lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an crucial mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

In a recent development, the connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

It has been revealed that yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

According to recent reports, "Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is vital because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

Sources indicate that "Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an notable role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo open-source infrastructure shield to prevent AI-driven cyberattacks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence.
  • Sources indicate that they’ve just unveiled a upcoming, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks.
  • In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:20 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

It has been revealed that cybercriminals have gained the ability to discover vulnerabilities in software and take advantage of them in seconds, and it’s all thanks to artificial intelligence. Enterprises need a better way to defend themselves, so it’s fitting that one of the world’s top AI companies, OpenAI Group PBC, together with Cisco Systems Inc., is stepping up with a solution.

Sources indicate that they’ve just unveiled a upcoming, open-source and extremely ambitious initiative called the Secure Infrastructure Project, which aims to ensure that all AI computing infrastructure is secure by design and capable of defending against lightning-fast AI-driven attacks. The first project within that initiative is Shirudo, which is designed to protect infrastructure systems automatically from critical exploits before they can be patched.

In a blog post, Cisco Security Chief Technology Officer and Vice President of Engineering Thomas Graf explained that the industry has always treated security as an afterthought, essentially something that’s bolted onto systems after the fact. It has gotten away with this because much of the world’s computing infrastructure was built for workflows that proceed at human speeds. But with the emergence of AI models that can discover and work out how to exploit vulnerabilities in a matter of seconds, this kind of reactive security is no longer enough.

According to recent reports, according to Graf, even now, when a major vulnerability is discovered in widely used software, it can take weeks or even months to come up with a fix and ensure that every major system is patched against it. “That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative, meaning that a growing number of vulnerabilities are now being exploited before they are publicly disclosed,” he said. “This will only accelerate with the further evolution of AI models and cybersecurity capabilities, becoming the norm in open-weight models.”.

To counter these kinds of automated attacks, Cisco and OpenAI believe that infrastructure has to be rebuilt from scratch with security in mind. They argue that it’s time to abandon static defenses and embrace systems that are hardened by default, immutable and rebuildable from a previous “good” state, so owners can quickly revert back in the event of an attack. To do this, infrastructure systems must be based on Trusted Platform Modules and utilize reinforcement learning techniques to safely test their own defenses so they can adapt when faced with novel cyberattacks from previously unknown vectors.

Graf said the key to doing this is to secure workloads at runtime, which is why the initial focus of Cisco’s and OpenAI’s initiative is Shirudo, an evolution of the open-source Tetragon runtime security project that aims to provide autonomous defense for AI agents.

Recent findings suggest that shirudo, named after the Japanese word for “shield,” is based on extended Berkeley Packet Filter or eBPF, which is a Linux kernel technology that acts like a kind of sandbox within the operating system. Similar to how JavaScript makes web browsers programmable without a restart, eBPF enables small, verified programs to run inside the Linux kernel to observe an application’s activity and modify its behavior without altering its source code or rebooting it.

Recent findings suggest that graf explained that Cisco and OpenAI chose to use eBPF because there are no other real alternatives. Human-focused security consoles and policy languages are simply too slow for AI agents, and will limit their productivity.

Industry observers note that by exposing programmable kernel interfaces, eBPF enables AI agents to capture granular telemetry, evaluate mitigations in monitoring mode and deploy cryptographically-signed shields in milliseconds. So cyberattacks that exploit unknown vulnerabilities can be blocked in real time without causing disruption to their live workloads.

“There is nothing more crucial than giving security teams the tools they need to match the speed of the AI-driven threats they are facing,” mentioned Cisco President and Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel. “We need self-defending infrastructure that acts at the speed of code, learns in real time and shields itself until patches are safely rolled out.”.

According to recent reports, openAI’s role in this is to prove that eBPF is up to the job, and it has already deployed Shirudo as part of an agentic control plane that’s powered by its Codex coding agent. When given details of a upcoming vulnerability, Codex can use Shirudo to autonomously build an exploit reproducer and then design a mitigation strategy. It then validates the mitigation code and deploys the cryptographically-signed shields across all affected nodes.

The two partners recently tested Shirudo against a critical new vulnerability in OpenJDK called Java4Shell, and it was able to rapidly generate Java bytecode that it injected directly into a running Elasticsearch agent to block malicious Base64 overwrites that would have compromised the system.

OpenAI co-founder and President Greg Brockman said the goal of Shirudo is to help companies protect their systems from new threats until they can build and deploy a more durable patch. “When one team finds a better way to protect a system, others shouldn’t have to start from scratch,” he explained.

To that end, Cisco and OpenAI say they’re welcoming developers, kernel engineers, platform builders and security experts to collaborate on Shirudo and other initiatives within their broader Secure Infrastructure Project.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, an international research team has developed a upcoming technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the newly introduced approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants.

According to recent reports, parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

Sources indicate that "The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers.".

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells.

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

It has been revealed that "We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces.".

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

In a recent development, "The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she indicates. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain.".

Industry observers note that the process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice.

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an notable target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease.".

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice demonstrated significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," claims Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

Recent findings suggest that "Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately.".

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a upcoming way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward fresh approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

Mom and Dad Survived 1980s Mortgage Rates. Here Is Why Buying a Home Today Is Still Much Harder.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1268 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It now takes the typical household 10.5 years to save for a down payment on a home—more than triple the time it took in the 1980s, according to a newly introduced analysis from Realtor.com®.
  • Industry observers note that it's a stark generational divide that may be hard to ignore this Thanksgiving.
  • For families sharing a roof, one seemingly innocent question could spark a much thornier conversation than intended: When are you going to buy a house?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It now takes the typical household 10.5 years to save for a down payment on a home—more than triple the time it took in the 1980s, according to a newly introduced analysis from Realtor.com®.

Industry observers note that it's a stark generational divide that may be hard to ignore this Thanksgiving. Roughly 1 in 3 young adults lived with their parents in 2025—a record 25.2 million Americans aged 18 to 34—according to separate research from Realtor.com. And the share rising the fastest is in regions long considered affordability havens.

For families sharing a roof, one seemingly innocent question could spark a much thornier conversation than intended: When are you going to buy a house?

Recent findings suggest that for parents who bought their first homes in the 1980s, the question might seem fair. After all, mortgage rates reached a record 18.63% in 1981, while inflation averaged 13.5% in 1980—compared to 7.28% and 3.7%, respectively, today.

But while older generations certainly faced obstacles of their own, those war stories don't fully capture the economics of today's market, claims Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com.

In a recent development, “The reality is that today's aspiring buyers face a different housing market than generations before,” she explains. “While mortgage rates were significantly higher in the 1980s, home prices were far more attainable relative to household incomes, allowing buyers to save for a down payment in a fraction of the time it takes today.”.

In a recent development, the impulse to look back at the 1980s for perspective on today's housing market is certainly understandable. But to Jones' point, these comparisons often overlook how dramatically home prices have climbed since "Back to the Future" first hit theaters.

Industry observers note that in the 1980s, the typical home cost about 3.2 times the median annual household income. Today, that ratio has climbed to 4.8, according to the Realtor.com analysis.

So even with mortgage rates well below their 1980s highs, today's households have approximately $150,000 less homebuying power than their counterparts four decades ago, according to the analysis.

And much of that divide has emerged within the past decade, giving individual and societal expectations little time to adjust.

As recently as 2019, the typical household needed 5.7 years to save for a 10% down payment. Today, that timeline has nearly doubled to 10.5 years.

Industry observers note that "Envision running in a race when your parents begin halfway to the finish. Everyone still expects you to reach the finish at the same time as they did," says Max Doshay, a clinical psychologist and co-founder and CEO of KMN Psych. “This is what comparisons of finances can be like for younger generations.”.

And the finish line has moved in more ways than one. Even after households save enough for a down payment, the resulting mortgage can remain out of reach.

In 43 of the nation's 50 largest metros, the estimated monthly mortgage payment on a median-priced home would consume more than 30% of median household income, even after putting 10% down, according to the metro-level calculations in the report.

Industry observers note that consider San Diego, where Doshay is based. There, the typical household would need an estimated 18.8 years to save for a 10% down payment of roughly $91,200.

Yet at today's prices and mortgage rates, the resulting $5,563 monthly payment would consume nearly 65% of median household income—more than twice the conventional 30% housing cost benchmark, even before accounting for property taxes or insurance.

Of course, it's hardly unreasonable for parents to want their children to enjoy the same security homeownership afforded them.

And the advantages of such security are well documented. Purchasing a home around age 30 was associated with 22.5% greater net worth by age 50—roughly $119,000 more—than buying in one's 40s, according to a March 2026 Realtor.com analysis.

The trouble begins when homeownership becomes more than a financial milestone, and the inability to reach it starts to feel like a symbol of personal failure.

“Homeownership has become such an integral part of what many consider to be successful in this country,” explains Bonnie Lambert, a board-certified psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner and licensed professional counselor at Crestview Recovery Center. “People buy houses so much because it makes them believe they are independent, responsible, and have accomplished something.”.

Those expectations can weigh on parents, too.

A whopping 71% of parents believe their adult children's successes and failures reflect at least a fair amount on the job they've done as parents, according to a 2024 Pew Research Center survey.

So, a child's struggle to buy a home may feel personal to parents, too. But what one generation expresses as concern, the other may hear as criticism.

Recent findings suggest that "Financial shame typically starts when someone simply thinks, 'I'm behind everyone else,'" Lambert says. "Whether it be because of seeing friends buying houses or hearing parents talk about how much property they had at our age, this comparison will leave us feeling embarrassed.".

And when those comparisons overlook how dramatically the economics have changed, frustration can turn inward.

"People who mistakenly view different beginning lines as failures make their frustrations about money into feelings of shame," Doshay claims. "They stop asking questions like 'Why are houses so expensive?' and instead ask themselves 'What's wrong with me?'".

That shame, in turn, can become another obstacle to overcome.

A 2021 study published in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, involving more than 9,000 participants across six studies, found evidence that financial shame can cause people to disengage from their finances, potentially reinforcing the difficulties that produced those feelings.

There's one more thing worth remembering before the conversation turns to homeownership this Thanksgiving: The struggle to buy a home isn't a reflection of how hard someone is trying.

"For many younger Americans, the challenge isn't a lack of willingness to save. It's that the financial goalposts have moved," Jones states.

And while recognizing those differences doesn't mean families have to avoid discussing money, how they approach those conversations can make all the difference.

"Well-meaning inquiries can be perceived as critical," Lambert claims.

"No one should ever have to go through an annual holiday dinner as their personal/financial review time," Doshay adds.

Rather than comparing financial milestones, he encourages parents to listen to their adult children. For those on the receiving end of uncomfortable questions, that may mean establishing boundaries.

Doshay suggests a response such as: "I am working on my objectives; however, I would prefer it if we did not talk about money today.".

It has been revealed that lambert, meanwhile, recommends shifting the focus away from homeownership as the ultimate measure of financial progress. Building savings or paying down debt can be accomplishments worth recognizing in their own right.

"No one else's timeline should ever dictate our deadlines for being happy," she says.

After all, parents can want their children to enjoy the same financial security they did without expecting them to reach it on the same schedule.

As Doshay puts it: "Owning a home is a financial obligation—it’s not proof you’ve reached maturity.".

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

Industry observers note that the Virginia Department of Health unveiled on Nov. 20 its first measles-associated death since 1978.

According to recent reports, the individual was a child younger than four years of age who had tested positive for measles, though the state has refrained from providing more information about the case for privacy reasons. The state has reported 220 cases in total this year, as of a Nov. 19 dashboard revision, with most occurring in its central region and at least 179 of which were confirmed to be unvaccinated.

Industry observers note that it is the fourth state this year to have reported a measles-associated death, following Pennsylvania, where a ninth death was reported on Monday, as well as Fresh York and Wisconsin. Pennsylvania's health department said it has now confirmed 1,638 cases across 46 of its counties this year, and noted that only five of those were among individuals vaccinated against the disease.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of a Nov. 19 enhancement, lists 5,838 confirmed cases of measles this year, well above 2025's total of 2,289. The agency has recognized six of the reported deaths as compared to states' 13, as the federal body said it is looking to develop a standardized definition for deaths due to measles amid disputes over the use and reporting of "measles-associated" deaths.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status, and has now exceeded 5,400 cases and 10 total measles-associated deaths in 2026.

According to recent reports, the status determination from the Pan American Health Organization, which is part of the World Health Organization, was made late last week and first reported by the Wall Street Journal before being confirmed by other outlets. (Editor's note: The public health body made its official announcement on Nov. 17).

The U.S. had notched elimination status, reflecting no continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months, in 2000. Regaining it similarly requires the country to stop continuous spread for 12 months. PAHO recommends countries that have lost elimination status submit and enact a corrective action strategy that includes immunization and surveillance.

The decision landed shortly after the country hit 5,412 confirmed measles cases, per a Nov. 13 update from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The federal public health body also lists 591 hospitalizations (11% rate) and six deaths—though it has been hesitant to outright confirm states' reports of measles-associated deaths, of which there have now been 10.

Health groups and public health professionals have pointed to lagging vaccination rates and checked endorsement of routine childhood vaccines from current leadership at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, namely Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as fueling the country's outbreaks.

The Wisconsin Department of Health Services on Thursday reported its first measles-outbreak associated death since 1990.

Industry observers note that the deceased was an infant whose case was among many in the southwestern part of the state, for whom the coroner listed measles as immediate cause of death. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 cases across 13 counties in 2026, the highest number of cases in over 35 years. All but three of those are among individuals who were not vaccinated, and nine have involved hospitalizations.

Industry observers note that "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease," Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in the announcement. "Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is vital for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.".

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone stated they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

The Upcoming York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

In a recent development, sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department noted. Many of Upcoming York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, Fresh York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease.".

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone noted they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a newly introduced standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles.".

A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services told Fierce Healthcare that it had deployed epidemiologists and other experts to Fresh York after receiving a formal request for support. The support is currently scheduled to run through Nov. 13, and includes on-the-ground "surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning and other outbreak response support," they said.

Of the roughly $100 million in additional measles and vaccine-preventable diseases funding the department has provided via the CDC since August, nearly $2.4 million has gone directly to New York State and $2.1 million to New York City, they noted.

Industry observers note that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles," they added.

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that the vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Industry observers note that measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Sources indicate that pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and latest CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not introduced the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Sources indicate that pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. Newly introduced York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, popular medications used to treat obesity and type 2 diabetes, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, may have effects that extend beyond weight loss and blood sugar control. These drugs also influence biological processes involved in brain function, raising questions about whether they could help preserve memory and thinking abilities.

To examine this possibility, researchers from the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen reviewed the existing scientific evidence at the invitation of the journal Science.

Recent findings suggest that studies involving animals suggest that GLP-1 medications can influence learning and memory. However, research involving humans has produced less consistent findings. Analyses of patient health records have found an association between GLP-1 treatment and a reduced risk of dementia among people with type 2 diabetes. These observational findings are encouraging, but they cannot determine whether the medications themselves are responsible for the lower risk.

Recent findings suggest that more definitive results have also raised questions. In Novo Nordisk's EVOKE and EVOKE+ clinical trials, semaglutide failed to slow the progression of early Alzheimer's disease. Although the treatment affected several biological markers associated with Alzheimer's, those changes did not translate into a measurable slowing of the disease.

Why Weight Loss Drugs May Still Benefit the Brain.

Despite the disappointing Alzheimer's results, researchers believe GLP-1 medications could still offer cognitive benefits to certain groups of patients.

People living with obesity or type 2 diabetes sometimes experience difficulties with attention, planning, and the speed at which they process information. These cognitive problems are often associated with metabolic health and blood vessel function, suggesting they may respond differently to treatment than the changes caused by Alzheimer's disease.

Improving blood sugar regulation, metabolism, or vascular health could potentially help preserve cognitive abilities, even if the same medications cannot slow an established neurodegenerative disease.

Stina Börchers, the review's first author and a researcher affiliated with both the University of Gothenburg and the University of Copenhagen, emphasizes the need to determine whether starting treatment earlier could make a difference.

According to recent reports, "We need to find out whether these treatments can help people with obesity or diabetes preserve their cognitive abilities, particularly if treatment begins before cognitive problems become established. It is also important to identify which patients might benefit," says Stina Börchers.

Unlocking New Treatments to Protect Memory.

Recent findings suggest that A central unanswered question is how GLP-1 medications might influence the brain. Their potential cognitive effects could result from improvements in metabolic health, direct actions within the brain, or a combination of both.

Understanding these mechanisms could help researchers identify which patients are most likely to benefit and potentially lead to medications designed specifically to support memory and other thinking abilities.

Christoffer Clemmensen, the review's senior author and a research group leader at the University of Copenhagen, sees an opportunity to use increasingly advanced obesity treatments to explore the connection between metabolism and the brain.

"Obesity medicines are becoming increasingly sophisticated, offering latest opportunities to understand how metabolic regulation influences brain function. By disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these drugs on the brain, we may ultimately be able to develop treatments specifically aimed at preserving cognitive function," says Christoffer Clemmensen.

It has been revealed that the researchers are calling for clinical trials that evaluate memory, attention, and other cognitive abilities beginning when patients first start treatment. Following these changes over time could help establish whether GLP-1 drugs genuinely protect brain function and clarify who might benefit most.

In a recent development, they also stress that treatment is not without potential drawbacks, particularly for older adults and people who are physically frail. Rapid weight loss can lead to a reduction in muscle mass, which may weaken physical function and offset some of the possible benefits.

Careful monitoring will therefore be essential as researchers investigate whether today's weight loss and diabetes medications could eventually provide upcoming ways to protect the brain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that crowdStrike Holdings Inc.
  • It has been revealed that the all-stock deal values the latter tech giant at $260.40 per share.
  • Investors weren’t entirely thrilled.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:29 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Sources indicate that crowdStrike Holdings Inc. today confirmed plans to acquire Zscaler Inc., a fellow provider of cybersecurity software, for about $43.9 billion.

It has been revealed that the all-stock deal values the latter tech giant at $260.40 per share. That’s a 34% premium to Zscaler’s closing price on Friday, the day CrowdStrike’s takeover interest became public. The transaction would be the largest cybersecurity acquisition on record by a wide margin.

Investors weren’t entirely thrilled. CrowdStrike’s shares fell 9% today, an indication that might think it’s an awfully large pill to swallow. Zscaler’s stock, however, rose almost 18%.

The companies reported their quarterly results in conjunction with the acquisition announcement. Both topped expectations across the board. CrowdStrike posted adjusted net income of $354.9 million on $1.58 billion in revenue, while Zscaler reported a $208.4 million adjusted profit and sales of $949.3 million. The former company also boosted its full-year guidance.

CrowdStrike’s flagship Falcon platform uses lightweight programs called sensors to protect employee devices, cloud instances and other technology assets. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange, in turn, protects the network connections that link together those assets. The platform is positioned as an alternative to virtual private network tools.

The product portfolios of CrowdStrike’s and Zscaler overlap in some areas. Both companies offer tools that can protect artificial intelligence applications from threats such as prompt injections. They also compete in the secure browser category, although their respective offerings take different approaches to blocking malware.

It has been revealed that zscaler offers a tool that can automatically launch simulated cyberattacks against applications to find weak points. CrowdStrike joined the fray as well earlier this year with SafeMind, a set of custom AI models and related assets. It not only finds software vulnerabilities but also develops detections, automated workflows designed to spot hacking attempts.

CrowdStrike said that it will use the network telemetry collected by Zscaler to enhance SafeMind’s training dataset. In 2024, the latter company disclosed that its platform blocked more than 9 billion threats per day. That activity, which has no doubt grown in volume since, should give CrowdStrike’s AI models a more complete understanding of hacker behavior.

In a recent development, the tech giant’s prepares for Zscaler also extend beyond AI training. CrowdStrike will incorporate the network protection provider’s software into its Flex offering, which enables customers to buy multiple cybersecurity tools via a single contract. That could help expand the adoption of Zscaler’s products among CrowdStrike customers.

Industry observers note that the companies have also identified other upselling opportunities. They disclosed today that about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet use CrowdStrike products.

It has been revealed that “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” noted CrowdStrike founder and Chief Executive Officer George Kurtz (pictured). “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen.”.

Industry observers note that crowdStrike expects to complete the acquisition in the second half of its 2028 fiscal year, which starts next February. The firm stated that the deal will be “significantly and immediately accretive” to free cash flow per share upon closing.

It has been revealed that crowdStrike expects Zscaler’s financial impact to grow over time. It estimates that the deal will unlock $500 million worth of annual cost synergies within 18 to 24 months, mainly in the form of data center, supplier and operational improvements. The tech giant also sees Zscaler boosting its annual revenue run-rate by $1 billion within 30 months.

#87719. Latest Update: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1093 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1093 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising difference in how the immune systems of males and females respond to obesity.
  • The discovery centers on eosinophils, immune cells best known for their involvement in allergies and asthma.
  • The study, published in PNAS Nexus, was led by University of California, Riverside biomedical scientists Meera Nair and Adam Godzik.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising difference in how the immune systems of males and females respond to obesity. Their findings suggest that certain immune cells found in body fat can help protect against inflammation and metabolic problems, while others may make these harmful effects worse.

The discovery centers on eosinophils, immune cells best known for their involvement in allergies and asthma. In experiments with mice, researchers found that these cells behave differently depending on biological sex, potentially helping explain why obesity does not affect males and females in the same way.

The study, published in PNAS Nexus, was led by University of California, Riverside biomedical scientists Meera Nair and Adam Godzik. Their findings challenge the longstanding assumption that eosinophils are largely similar cells with relatively few specialized functions. The results also point toward potential new approaches for treating obesity and its complications.

Six Types of Immune Cells Found in Body Fat.

Sources indicate that to investigate the role of eosinophils in obesity, the researchers used high-resolution single-cell sequencing, a technique that allows scientists to examine gene activity in individual cells. They identified six distinct eosinophil populations in adipose (fat) tissue, each with its own pattern of gene expression and potentially different biological functions.

This unexpected diversity suggests that eosinophils play a much more complicated role in metabolic health than previously recognized.

"Eosinophils are more complex than we once thought," mentioned Nair, a professor of biomedical sciences in the UCR School of Medicine. "Some populations can protect against obesity, and if we can identify and activate the pathways that produce these protective cells, we may find newly introduced ways to improve metabolic health.".

Why Male and Female Fat Tissue Respond Differently.

One of the most striking discoveries was a difference in the immune cells found in male and female mice.

Recent findings suggest that female mice possessed a protective population of eosinophils that appeared to communicate more effectively with macrophages, another group of immune cells present in fat tissue. According to Nair, this cooperation may help create a healthier environment within fat tissue and support better metabolic function.

Male mice indicated a different pattern. When given a diet high in fat, they were more likely to develop eosinophil populations associated with inflammation. Their fat tissue also contained eosinophils with gene activity patterns suggesting weaker protective functions.

It has been revealed that these findings indicate that the effects of eosinophils on obesity depend on more than simply how many of these cells are present. The particular type of eosinophil and its interactions with neighboring immune cells may be equally important.

"This means the relationship between eosinophils and obesity is not simply a matter of how many eosinophils are present," mentioned Rebecca E. Ruggiero-Ruff, a postdoctoral researcher in Nair's lab and co-first author of the paper. "Their functional characteristics and how they communicate with other immune cells are also critical.".

A Protein That May Help Protect Against Inflammation.

The researchers also identified a protein called RELM alpha that appears to play an important role in maintaining the beneficial relationship between eosinophils and macrophages.

Sources indicate that produced by macrophages, RELM alpha seemed to help stabilize communication between the two immune cell types in female mice. This interaction may be one reason certain eosinophil populations are better able to support healthy fat tissue.

The finding builds on earlier experiments by the same research group, which showed that administering RELM alpha to mice produced protective effects. Together, the results suggest that the protein may help regulate immune activity within fat tissue and influence how the body responds to obesity.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Obesity Treatments?

Although the results offer fresh insight into the biology of obesity, the experiments were conducted in mice. Researchers have also detected eosinophils in fat tissue from people with obesity, but scientists do not yet fully understand what these cells do in the human body.

Nair cautioned that additional research will be necessary before the discovery can be used to develop treatments. One particularly notable question is whether therapies targeting the immune system would work differently in men and women.

"A drug may not activate the same pathways or produce the same effects in males and females, particularly when it targets the immune system," said co-first author Xinru Qiu, a postdoctoral researcher in Godzik's lab. "We need to investigate sex-specific biology more thoroughly so that treatments can be optimized for different patients.".

Understanding these differences could eventually help researchers design more personalized treatments for obesity and the metabolic complications associated with it.

Scientists Blueprint to Recreate Human Fat Tissue in the Lab.

The research team is now investigating whether the protective behavior observed in mouse eosinophils can also be studied in human laboratory models.

According to recent reports, to accomplish this, the scientists are developing three-dimensional adipose organoids. These miniature laboratory models reproduce certain features of real fat tissue, allowing researchers to examine how eosinophils interact with fat cells and other components of their environment.

The goal is to determine whether changing communication between immune cells could encourage healthier responses in human fat tissue.

According to recent reports, "We ultimately hope to develop human adipose organoids that will allow us to investigate whether manipulating immune-cell communication can promote healthier tissue responses," noted Godzik, a professor of biomedical sciences and the Bruce D. and Nancy B. Varner Presidential Endowed Chair in Cancer Research.

The findings raise the possibility that targeting specific immune cell populations, rather than treating all eosinophils as functionally identical, could eventually provide upcoming ways to address obesity and its complications. Whether the same protective mechanisms operate in humans remains an notable question for future research.

The research team also included Lauren Vance, Yuxin He, and Djurdjica Coss, who worked alongside Nair, Godzik, Ruggiero-Ruff, and Qiu.

Funding for the study came from the National Institutes of Health, the UCR School of Medicine, and the California Institute for Regenerative Medicine.

The research paper is titled "Single-cell heterogeneity of adipose eosinophils is shaped by sex and RELMα and linked to macrophage communication networks in obesity.".
