💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that’s been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks.
  • Industry observers note that at HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago.
  • Sources indicate that rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seesaw pattern for mortgage rates that’s been the story for much of the second half of 2026 reared its head again this week as rates for major loan types declined, reversing some of the increases from prior weeks.

Industry observers note that at HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.53% — down 5 basis points from a week ago. Rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) dropped 7 bps to 7.30%, while rates for 30-year jumbo loans plummeted 25 bps to 7.62%.

Sources indicate that rates in the mid-7% range continue to weigh on homebuyer demand and affordability metrics. Last week’s application index from the Mortgage Bankers Association indicated that total applications were down 5% on a weekly basis. MBA data released Tuesday found that affordability is about 8% weaker than a year ago, even though it improved slightly from September to October.

“Higher mortgage rates weighed on application activity last week, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.35%. Purchase applications were down 18% from a year ago, reflecting continued affordability challenges and softer homebuyer demand. The direction of mortgage rates in the coming weeks will be key to the housing market’s momentum heading into 2027,” MBA president and CEO Bob Broeksmit said in a statement.

In a recent development, dan Ribler, vice president of capital markets and strategy at national reverse mortgage lender Longbridge Financial, remarked that the October jobs report should’ve sent rates higher. Nonfarm payrolls increased by 165,000 positions last month and the unemployment rate remained steady at 4.1%, indicative of today’s healthier labor market conditions in relation to 2025.

Ribler noted that the jobless rate has been below 5% every month since September 2021, unemployment claims are lower than a year ago and the Federal Reserve‘s “own description is the labor market is very strong.” But strong employment trends have been overshadowed by stubborn inflation, which continues to run well above the central bank’s 2% annualized target.

“Inflation has been above 2% year over year 57 months in a row,” Ribler remarked. “The Fed has, by the way, under this administration, reiterated the 2% hurdle and that they’re going to be tough on inflation. They’re certainly talking the hawk talk, saying we’re going to keep inflation under 2%.

“But man, I don’t know about you, if my kid breaks curfew 57 nights in a row — and I say I’m going to punish you one of these times and I never do anything about it — at some point, he stops believing me, right?”.

It has been revealed that inflation is likely to prompt the Fed to raise rates next month. The CME Group‘s FedWatch tool reveals that a 25-bps hike in December is all but certain, with 96% of interest rate traders saying that the federal funds rate will rise to a range of 4% to 4.25%. It was last at that level in September 2025.

Much of the housing and mortgage industry headlines in the past week have cast a shadow over any potential market improvements in 2027.

Recent findings suggest that selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, mentioned in a statement that existing home sales have fallen to their lowest level since August 2010. She also pointed to a Realtor.com analysis, which found that the typical repeat buyer will pay about $1,100 more per month if they choose to sell and move.

“A meaningful housing recovery requires rates to come down and, importantly, stay down long enough to improve affordability and unlock turnover,” Hepp said. “Until then, the adjustment is likely to come through weaker sales and softer home prices rather than widespread homeowner distress.

Industry observers note that “The number worth writing is the $1,100. That’s the jump in monthly payment a typical repeat buyer takes on just to move house. It’s the clearest explanation yet of why nobody is selling.”.

According to recent reports, new home sales have been equally grim, with September’s seasonally adjusted annual rate of 676,000 sales representing a 5.3% decline from a year ago. Higher rates have also prompted homebuilders to remain cautious about creating more supply, with U.S. Census Bureau figures showing that single-family housing starts were down 3.2% year over year in September. Monthly gains in total starts were largely tied to the multifamily sector.

“Challenging affordability has been weighing on the resale market. Newly pending sales fell 17% in October, the largest year-over-year drop since 2023,” Zillow senior economist Kenny Lee said in a statement. “Single-family homebuilders have been navigating the same challenge. While homebuilders have been adapting to the softer market by offering concessions and building smaller homes, the 2027 spring home-shopping season could see a slow start as buyer demand continues to wane.”.

The relative lack of sales has weighed on mortgage origination volumes, with ATTOM data for the third quarter of 2026 showing that the roughly 730,000 purchase loans closed during that period were the lowest figure for any third quarter in 14 years.

Industry observers note that refinance activity was also bleak, with the roughly 561,000 refis in Q3 down 19% year over year. Refi lending was down from Q2 2026 in nearly 90% of the metro areas analyzed by ATTOM, with the largest declines in major metros like San Jose, San Francisco, Dallas, Austin and Louisville, Kentucky.

  • The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

According to recent reports, sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Latest America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

In a recent development, sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates remarked Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

Industry observers note that she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

Recent findings suggest that in its own analysis, The Newly introduced York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates remarked she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

FHFA raises conforming loan limit to $855,400 in 2027

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (469 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA).
  • The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates.
  • Under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The baseline conforming loan limit will rise 2.71% in 2027 to $855,400 for one-unit properties in most parts of the country, according to the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA). Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will be authorized to buy loans up to that balance in the vast majority of U.S. counties.

The $855,400 cap is an increase of $22,650 from 2026 and reflects slower home price growth tied to a weaker housing market and higher-for-longer mortgage rates. The annual adjustment was 3.25% last year and above 5% in each of the prior two years.

Under the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008 (HERA), the national “ceiling” for high-cost areas is set at 150% of the baseline. For 2027, that ceiling will be $1,283,100 for one-unit properties in markets where 115% of the local median home value exceeds the baseline limit. Conforming caps first surpassed $1 million in these high-cost areas in 2022.

Special statutory provisions apply in Alaska, Hawaii, Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands. In these areas, the 2027 baseline loan limit for one-unit properties will be $1,283,100, while the ceiling will be $1,924,650.

Sources indicate that “Due to rising home values, the CLL will be higher in all but 24 U.S. counties or county equivalents,” the FHFA stated in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that each November, FHFA publishes fresh conforming loan limits for the coming year. Increases resumed in 2016, after home prices returned to pre-Great Recession levels, a condition required by HERA. The statute also prevents the ceiling from declining in years when home prices fall; the cap only moves higher when national prices increase year over year.

According to recent reports, this year’s adjustment is tied to FHFA’s third-quarter 2026 House Price Index (HPI), which tracks changes in average U.S. home values over the prior four quarters. Nominal, seasonally adjusted, expanded-data HPI showed house prices rose 2.72% on average between the third quarters of 2025 and 2026, essentially matching the 2.71% rise in the baseline conforming loan limit.

According to recent reports, the latest limits expand the amount of mortgage debt that can qualify for conventional financing backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Loans above FHFA’s limits are classified as jumbos, a segment still dominated by banks and portfolio lenders that set their own credit standards and capital requirements.

Mortgage lenders once again anticipated FHFA’s announcement and raised their internal conforming loan limits ahead of the official release to compete for volume. But they were conservative.

Rocket Mortgage was an early mover, lifting its conforming loan limit to $845,000 for single-family homes in 48 states in September. CrossCountry Mortgage adopted the same level.

Pennymac set its internal limit at $850,000, while United Wholesale Mortgage increased its one-unit cap for conventional and Department of Veterans Affairs loans to $847,440.

  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • In a recent development, terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

In a recent development, terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the manufacturer’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Recent findings suggest that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Recent findings suggest that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Sources indicate that users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

According to recent reports, howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it debuted publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of people. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BlackRock, the leading asset management firm and Bitcoin’s largest ETF issuer, sparked discussions earlier today following a massive Bitcoin sale by the manufacturer.

The latest data showcased by SosoValue shows that the leading Bitcoin fund has witnessed massive single-day withdrawals from investors who have ventured into its Bitcoin investment product.

Earlier today, BlackRock sold over half a billion dollars’ worth of Bitcoin after its spot Bitcoin ETF, also known as iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), recorded a total of $541.08 million in net outflows.

This massive outflow has come as Bitcoin’s price decline continues to intensify, causing investors to aggressively pull their money out of the fund amid growing market fear.

While this marks the third time this week that BlackRock has recorded a net outflow amid persistent market volatility, it also marks the largest single-day outflow BlackRock has recorded since its launch.

Apparently, the record-breaking withdrawal that the fund just witnessed suggests that institutional and traditional investors are becoming less willing to retain their exposure to Bitcoin through asset managers, especially as Bitcoin’s price continues to slump further.

Although BlackRock has just suffered the largest withdrawal since it launched its Bitcoin investment product, the record outflow did not alter its dominance in the market.

Further data demonstrates that the BlackRock spot Bitcoin ETF still boasts a massive $47.82 billion in assets under management, spotlighting its leadership in the Bitcoin ETF market.

This positions it far ahead of Fidelity, which ranks as the second-largest Bitcoin ETF with just $10.62 billion in net assets.

#87616. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that taylor Swift, classical or silence?
  • It has been revealed that ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers.
  • Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

It has been revealed that ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Sources indicate that ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in Upcoming York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

Sources indicate that “Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”.

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be remarked for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Industry observers note that megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan remarked. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”.

Recent findings suggest that jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

It has been revealed that “Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”.

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s right now listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”.

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

In a recent development, daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Industry observers note that natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

In a recent development, “By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”.

Industry observers note that for mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

Industry observers note that “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

According to recent reports, she leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She claims music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”.

Recent findings suggest that hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he indicates, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

In a recent development, he also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”.

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”.

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

In a recent development, shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea claims she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”.

It has been revealed that marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, Fresh Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

Industry observers note that “Every week, I share latest songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”.

Recent findings suggest that on setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she noted.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova mentioned she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

According to recent reports, so the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova stated, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”.

Fluidstack engineers and designs data centers in the U.S., then assembles them on construction sites across the country, so American companies can build AI infrastructure here at speed," noted Gary Wu, CEO of Fluidstack. "That's how we keep American leadership in AI. And we're just getting started.".

Fluidstack designs, engineers, integrates, and sells all products in the United States and intends to deliver them finished and tested from a single source.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.
  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really significant step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Industry observers note that nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles remarked.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles noted. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “crucial step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson stated in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

According to recent reports, next year, Zeno Power aims to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

Industry observers note that the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The manufacturer is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Recent findings suggest that exposure management company Astelia Inc. today announced the launch of autonomous network mitigation, a fresh capability that allows organizations to block artificial intelligence-driven exploits at the network level, even when a patch isn’t available or can’t be applied.

According to recent reports, the new capability has been designed to address what Astelia claims is the problem of frontier AI models cutting the time to exploit to almost zero, leaving manual triage and remediation unable to keep up. Astelia argues that autonomous remediation isn’t a viable option for large enterprises, where every patch requires a change window so it doesn’t break vital business processes. In many cases, there is also no patch to apply because the vendor hasn’t released a fix yet or, for older and end-of-life systems, never will.

“For years, security teams have been told to patch faster,” noted co-founder and Chief Executive Alon Noy, adding that the advice “stops working when the exploit arrives before the change window does.”.

In a recent development, autonomous network mitigation is designed to block the path an attacker would use to reach a vulnerable system instead of changing the system itself. Mitigations are applied automatically within policies the organization sets. Nothing on the asset is changed, allowing business-critical systems, including operational technology, to stay online.

Underpinning the service is Astelia’s reachability analysis, which maps an organization’s real network topology and applies agentic AI to analyze the requirements of each exploit. By correlating exploit conditions with network topology, the platform identifies which vulnerabilities are reachable by attackers and through which paths. In one enterprise deployment, approximately 40 million vulnerabilities were reduced to fewer than 2,000 that were reachable, according to the tech giant.

Sources indicate that key features of autonomous network mitigation include the ability to identify the most effective choke point on an attack path and drive the mitigation through an organization’s web application firewall or intrusion prevention and detection system. A single rule at a choke point is remarked to protect every vulnerable server behind it, compared with one change per server when patching. Because mitigations are only applied to paths that have been proven reachable, the service doesn’t add rules for exposure that doesn’t exist.

In a recent development, every mitigation applied by Astelia can also be rolled back, something that isn’t always possible with a patch. That is said to allow teams to act quickly without putting business operations at risk.

Recent findings suggest that autonomous network mitigation can be deployed through Astelia Agents, the tech giant’s suite of AI agents, as a dedicated agent that applies mitigations on its own. The agent can also be connected with other agents to respond to urgent threats such as zero-day vulnerabilities and critical disclosures. Astelia gave the example of the PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws disclosed in October, which left end-of-life PHP servers with no official fix.

Each organization sets its own guardrails on how mitigations are applied. Consumers can require human approval for specific environments or actions, according to the company. Every action is logged and can be audited. Analysis on the Astelia platform continues to run on read-only integrations, with mitigation actions using scoped permissions that each organization enables and controls.

Autonomous network mitigation initially supports web application firewall and intrusion prevention and detection rules, with support for firewall rules planned in the future.

Founded in 2024 by former leaders of the Israeli National Red Team, Astelia is a venture capital-backed company that raised $35 million in combined seed and Series A funding in February. Investors in the company include Index Ventures, Team8 and Holly Ventures.

Three XRP Ledger amendments linked to native lending have each gained two validator votes since Nov. 17, according to XRPScan data. As of Nov. 20, 2026, Single Asset Vault (XLS-65) had 25 votes, and Lending Protocol (XLS-66) and the LendingProtocolV1_1 patch had 24 votes each.

XRPScan data shows that LendingProtocolV1_1 has been up for a vote since Sept. 29, 2026, when it came with the v3.4.0 release. According to the patch's voting history, it had about 19 votes for most of October. It started to gain votes again in late October. XRP was trading at $0.96 on Friday.

Lending is built directly into the XRP Ledger's code, with no third-party smart contracts. According to Ripple, lenders deposit into a Single Asset Vault, and the Lending Protocol lets loan brokers use that capital "to matter loans and track repayments onchain.".

In a recent development, the model is close to how banks lend. Loans have fixed terms and a repayment schedule, and credit brokers vet borrowers before the loans are issued. On Nov. 19, Clearpool revealed the full lending flow on the XRPL Devnet with Ripple's RLUSD stablecoin. In the demo, "An approved lender funds a private vault, and a borrower accepts and repays a loan underwritten offchain by a broker," Clearpool wrote.

Recent findings suggest that through Single Asset Vault (XLS-65), XRP holders will be able to deposit their coins into shared liquidity pools, and institutional borrowers will take loans from those pools at a fixed rate. After the loan is repaid, "the lender redeems at a higher share price," according to the Clearpool demo.

The amendments still need more votes before they can activate. "An amendment needs more than 80% support, held for 14 days, to activate," XRPScan indicates on its amendment pages. For the current set of 35 validators, the site puts the threshold at "more than 80% of 35 votes, so 29 needed.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the FICO 10T credit score model for use by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. It also released an implementation road map that would make FICO 10T broadly eligible and retire Classic FICO by September 2028.

The staged rollout, confirmed Tuesday, mirrors the VantageScore 4.0 timeline and is meant to give lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers time to analyze historic FICO 10T data, rework pricing and risk models, and enhancement technology before a full transition, according to the agency.“The timeline below prepares lenders, mortgage insurers and loan origination system providers for the final step in credit score modernization: lender choice between FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0,” the agency said. At the Federal Housing Administration (FHA), VantageScore 4.0 and FICO 10T are expected to go live alongside the existing Classic FICO in January.

Bob Broeksmit, president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), issued a statement of support following the announcement.

It has been revealed that “We welcome this milestone as it moves us closer to the industry’s and FHFA’s goal of transitioning to true competition with two modernized credit score models,” Broeksmit remarked. “We appreciate FHFA’s desire to provide a clear and transparent roadmap for this process. Given the industry’s experience with the just-completed adoption of VantageScore 4.0, MBA will work with FHFA and industry stakeholders to expedite the implementation timeline responsibly.

Industry observers note that “MBA and its members will continue to engage with FHFA to establish meaningful competition for both credit scoring and credit reporting. Continued reforms to end the tri-merge requirement will further improve our credit reporting system and lower costs for borrowers. Today’s announcement is a critical next step.”.

The FHFA initially validated both FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0 for use at the government-sponsored (GSEs) enterprises in October 2022. In July 2026, Fannie and Freddie released historical performance data for FICO 10T along with additional VantageScore 4.0 data, a key prerequisite for lenders and investors to back-test new score models and recalibrate credit policy.A FICO 10T pilot is expected to begin around December 2027. In this “launch and refine” phase, lenders will deliver a subset of loans underwritten with FICO 10T while FHFA, the GSEs and industry stakeholders monitor data quality, pricing and delivery performance.

According to recent reports, based on pilot results, FHFA expects upfront pricing grids and private mortgage insurer eligibility requirements, or PMIERs, to be updated to reflect the new score model. That step will be critical for secondary market execution and risk transfer structures that presently rely on Classic FICO.

A limited FICO 10T rollout is targeted for April 2028, followed by a scale-up and transition phase that leads to broad eligibility around September 2028. During this final stage, FHFA plans to confirm industry readiness, fully implement Uniform Loan Delivery Dataset (ULDD) Phase 5, expand FICO 10T use across GSE channels and retire Classic FICO.

FHFA emphasized that dates after November 2026 are targets and are subject to change.

In October, Fair Isaac Corp. noted it will hold its wholesale mortgage price at $10 for a bundle of its credit scores for lenders and brokers enrolled in its Preferred Program. The $10 price is available through participating tri-merge credit report resellers to lenders that commit to FICO under the program. It covers both Classic FICO, which has been the mortgage standard for nearly three decades, and FICO Score 10T, the company’s trended-data model.

FICO is also preparing a latest subscription-based pricing model for mortgage credit scores in 2027, sources told HousingWire.

VantageScore 4.0, by comparison, has been offered at 99 cents per score, or at no additional charge when purchased alongside a FICO score through Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, which jointly own VantageScore.

Bank of America Global Research, using data from Recursion, found that more than 170 lenders now pull VantageScore 4.0. Despite that breadth of use, only a small share of conventional loans are actually priced with VantageScore 4.0. In October, 20% of issuance reported a VantageScore 4.0, yet only about 8% of total issuance used the score model for pricing, according to the research.

Editor’s note: This story was updated with a statement from the MBA.

  • According to recent reports, for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

According to recent reports, for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The tech giant started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Sources indicate that beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond manufacturer agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Sources indicate that listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

Sources indicate that the five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei noted Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the tech giant to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

It has been revealed that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

What will Social Security look like in 2027 and beyond?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, swiftly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.
  • Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently revealed 3.6% COLA for 2027.
  • Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, swiftly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.

Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently revealed 3.6% COLA for 2027. But Morningstar noted this week that the 2027 COLA — the largest since 2023’s 8.7% adjustment — will translate into smaller take-home increases once Medicare costs are deducted.

Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks. Morningstar reported that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 next year to $209.40, a 3.2% increase. That will allow most beneficiaries to keep more than 3% of the 3.6% COLA after the deduction.

Industry observers note that morningstar calculated that a retiree receiving the average October benefit of $2,092 would see a net benefit increase of about 3.29%, assuming they pay the standard Part B premium and have no other changes in deductions. A higher-income retiree with a $3,500 monthly benefit would see a net increase of roughly 3.41% under the same assumptions.

It has been revealed that the COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which compares the average readings for July, August and September on a year-over-year basis. Analysts cited by Morningstar noted that CPI-W may understate seniors’ actual cost pressures, particularly for healthcare, and pointed to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI-E index for older households, which has historically risen faster than CPI-W.

In a recent development, the Senior Citizens League (TSCL) noted the projected 3.6% COLA for 2028 is likely to arrive against a deteriorating backdrop for older adults, including senior homeowners who may still be making monthly mortgage payments. The group said that seniors are now the country’s fastest-growing homeless population and that many forgo vision, dental and hearing care due to costs.

Industry observers note that TSCL’s release emphasized that Social Security’s primary trust fund is projected to reach insolvency in 2032, triggering automatic benefit reductions if Congress does not act. The Medicare Part A hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, the group stated.

In a recent development, that timing elevates the stakes for the next Congress, which will be led by Democrats after their decisive victories in the recent midterm elections. Senators elected in the current cycle will serve from Jan. 3, 2027, through Jan. 3, 2033, overlapping the projected insolvency date. TSCL framed these terms as a key window for any reforms to prevent automatic benefit cuts for millions of retirees.

In its agenda for the 120th Congress, TSCL called on lawmakers to:.

Recent findings suggest that TSCL pointed to Social Security Administration projections, which show that eliminating the taxable wage cap would add “decades” to the trust fund’s life. And the organization’s internal polling indicates broad bipartisan support among seniors for lifting the cap.

As advocacy groups push for revenue-raising reforms, a new proposal in the Senate would instead rely on federal borrowing to preserve full benefits.

Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, has introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. The bill would allow the Department of the Treasury to transfer general fund dollars to Social Security’s retirement trust fund once it becomes insolvent, according to a press release published last week by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB).

Industry observers note that under current law, Social Security can only pay benefits from dedicated payroll tax income and trust fund reserves. When the retirement trust fund’s reserves are exhausted — presently projected to be in less than six years — benefits would be cut by about 22% without legislative changes.

CRFB estimated that backfilling Social Security with general revenue under Johnson’s bill would increase federal debt by $190 trillion over the next 75 years on an inflation-adjusted basis, equal to roughly 165% of gross domestic product.

“Paying for Social Security out of the general fund would absolutely explode the national debt, costing a whopping 165% of GDP over 75 years before even considering the economic implications,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas stated in the release, arguing that the policy could trigger a debt crisis or unsettle bond markets even before it is fully implemented.

CRFB characterized the bill as avoiding “the real decisions” needed to repair Social Security’s finances and urged lawmakers to pursue a mix of adjustments — potentially through a bipartisan commission — that would close the program’s funding gap without shifting the shortfall onto the federal balance sheet.

The trajectory of Social Security and Medicare benefits has direct implications for housing demand and credit risk among the senior segment.

Industry observers note that net benefit increases closer to 3% than 3.6% may constrain seniors’ ability to absorb higher housing costs — including the required property tax, insurance and association dues associated with reverse mortgages. The impact could be particularly acute in housing markets with rapid property tax growth.

It has been revealed that rising healthcare and prescription costs could drive more senior homeowners to tap their equity through home sales or reverse mortgages. Increased levels of downsizing would alter inventory and product mixes in senior-heavy markets.

According to recent reports, A 22% across-the-board benefit cut in the next decade, if Congress fails to act, would likely raise delinquency risks among fixed-income borrowers and could affect investor views of senior-heavy mortgage-backed securities pools. Conversely, large-scale borrowing to backfill Social Security, as proposed in Johnson’s bill, could influence interest rates and broader funding conditions.

It has been revealed that localized affordability pressures could also emerge. Growth in senior homelessness and medical cost burdens might increase demand for affordable and supportive housing. It could also influence municipal planning, tax policy and zoning decisions that shape housing development pipelines.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.
  • Sources indicate that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005.
  • Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents remarked.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO mentioned he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint stated he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”.

White also allegedly mentioned that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton noted it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”.

It has been revealed that pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also stated the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

Sources indicate that “NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”.

Visualized with the help of AI.

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”.

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

According to recent reports, pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”.

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious strategy to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.
  • Sources indicate that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

Sources indicate that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

Sources indicate that he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

It has been revealed that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek stated. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Industry observers note that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he noted. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

Industry observers note that after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk tech giant developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

Recent findings suggest that “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

According to recent reports, redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

Recent findings suggest that in 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in fresh natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who remarked the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he remarked, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

It has been revealed that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion organization Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

In a recent development, A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

Recent findings suggest that while the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The organization landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd remarked he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

It has been revealed that endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd noted there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

In a recent development, the manufacturer now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

Recent findings suggest that “This was always the end goal,” Redd remarked. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

PASADENA, Calif., Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- PrismML today unveiled Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an upgrade to the Ternary Bonsai 2 27B with substantially stronger agentic coding and multi-turn tool use. The model is based on Qwen3.8 27B, sits at 5.9GB memory, and retains or exceeds the benchmark scores of its predecessor, giving developers a strong foundation for coding and knowledge work agents that run on personal devices.

According to recent reports, across agentic coding benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified, DeepSWE v1.1, and Terminal-Bench 2.1), Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieved an average score of 54.2, compared to 37.9 for Ternary Bonsai 2 27B. Across agentic tool-calling benchmarks (AppWorld and ÏÂ³-Bench), Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B achieved an average score of 82.2, compared to 60.2 for Ternary Bonsai 2 27B. Full results and evaluation settings are available in the accompanying whitepaper.

Preserving capability across longer tasks.

Agentic workloads are particularly demanding for compressed models. Small errors can compound across successive tool calls, causing an agent to lose track of its objective or repeat unsuccessful approaches. Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B addresses these limitations, significantly narrowing the performance gap to the full-precision model on longer, multi-step tasks.

In a recent development, development focused on how the model responds as a task unfolds: incorporating tool feedback, recovering from failed actions, and avoiding unnecessary reasoning and unproductive repetition. The goal is to help agents complete work more reliably, with fewer wasted steps, lower token use, and shorter execution times.

In a recent development, "Getting a capable model onto a device is only part of the challenge," said Babak Hassibi, Founder and CEO of PrismML. "It also has to remain effective through all the decisions involved in completing a real complex task. That is where we focused our work with Bonsai 2.5.".

From private codebases to everyday knowledge work.

The release expands the scope of work developers can build local agents to handle. A coding assistant can inspect a private repository, make changes, run the relevant tests, and use the results to refine its fix, all within the developer's local environment. A knowledge work assistant can turn a folder of documents into a structured analysis, reconcile inconsistent records, or prepare a repeatable workflow for recurring reports. These assignments require sustained execution across files and tools. Stronger performance over longer interactions makes more of this work practical to delegate.

It has been revealed that for product teams, this makes it easier to embed capable agents directly into their applications, using existing context and tools while keeping model inference and sensitive information on the user's device. PrismML also works with developers on domain-specific post-training and inference optimization to tailor these capabilities to their applications and target hardware.

Recent findings suggest that ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B uses ternary weights to deliver 27B-class capabilities in a compact 5.9 GB model footprint. It runs on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs through llama.cpp and on Apple devices, including Mac, iPhone, and iPad, through MLX.

Technical details of PrismML's compression, evaluation, and benchmarking processes are available in the manufacturer's whitepaper.

Developers, researchers, and other users can download the Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B model under the Apache 2.0 license for free starting November 24, 2026.
