📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:23 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places fresh demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

Industry observers note that “I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”.

Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:.

Enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

Industry observers note that “Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he said during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”.

Recent findings suggest that the demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

According to recent reports, “What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:.

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing upcoming AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

Industry observers note that “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most vital thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

In a recent development, “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most crucial thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

Industry observers note that the integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

According to recent reports, “Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole mentioned during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”.

Another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

“AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he mentioned during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:.

As enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

Recent findings suggest that “Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”.

Automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability glitch,” she said during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Helen Yu and Sandeep Singh:.

The Counterintuitive Sales Strategy That Built My Business

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1106 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • By all accounts, I was a phenomenal salesperson.
  • It has been revealed that when you’re selling inside a large organization with a seven-figure quota, there are things you simply have to do to hit your numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

By all accounts, I was a phenomenal salesperson. I always exceeded my quota, which in the sales world meant that my quota increased every year. But just because I was effective doesn’t mean that I loved it.

It has been revealed that when you’re selling inside a large organization with a seven-figure quota, there are things you simply have to do to hit your numbers. For me, that meant pushing and pitching to just about anyone who would listen, and it took a heavy toll on my mental health.

In a recent development, the toll came from feeling that I had to do things that didn’t align with my ethics or my entrepreneurial beliefs. In the seven years I’ve run my agency, I haven’t had to compromise my ethics to build a book of business or grow my pipeline. Instead, I’ve focused on what I call selling by helping.

Recent findings suggest that rather than pushing and pitching at every opportunity, I found places where my ideal clients were raising their hands and asking for help, and I simply offered to help them. Only a small fraction of the people I’ve helped have ended up needing my service. But the ones who did were exactly the people my business was built to serve, and the ones who got the most value from it.

As AI makes sales outreach more automated, I believe this human approach will matter more than ever. Here’s how to put it into practice — and the tool I’d recommend to support it.

However advanced AI gets, buyers will still want to deal with real humans. A recent study conducted by HubSpot and SurveyMonkey found that 82% of consumers prefer human support, even when outcomes and wait times are the same. Trust is built through relationships, and relationships are ultimately rooted in human connection. Even before AI, plenty of companies failed to make selling feel human.

Sources indicate that that was the part of the sales profession I disliked most — and the part I resisted when I was selling full-time. It’s also why selling by helping is the opposite of the impersonal approach so common in modern sales. The RAIN Group Center for Sales Research found that 96% of buyers say a seller’s focus on the value they can deliver influences their purchase decision. Furthermore, 90% of organizations classified as value-driven experienced year-over-year revenue growth, compared to 72% of organizations that weren’t value-driven.

As you have more conversations focused on genuinely helping someone, resist the urge to turn your help into a quid pro quo. Lead with value instead of trying to extract it. When you do, what comes back to you is worth far more than anything you could have extracted.

It has been revealed that in practice, that means knowing when to end the conversation. Imagine you’ve just had a great conversation with someone who looks like an ideal client, and you’ve really helped them. In a traditional sales environment, that’s when you’d pitch. With selling by helping, you end the conversation once you’ve added value. No chasing, no pitching and no pushing anyone toward a sale.

That doesn’t mean you forget about them. Remember who they are, build a natural connection and stay in touch, always by adding value. The payoff is that when they need the service you offer, you’ll be top of mind. At least, that has been my experience. That’s how you sell like a human.

Sources indicate that my organization works in the Salesforce ecosystem and has a free app on the AppExchange, so we have Salesforce licenses in-house. But I use a CRM far less than I did when I was selling full-time. When you’re leading with value, it doesn’t matter whether you track relationships in a CRM, an Excel sheet or a notebook. The tool won’t change your approach to selling.

The one place I have found worth investing in is LinkedIn. I tell the founders I coach that they don’t need a website to launch a solo agency. They need a LinkedIn presence that makes it obvious who they help and how.

It has been revealed that that’s where LinkedIn Premium Business comes in. It lets you showcase what you offer on your own service page, share client testimonials and collect reviews as you build your business. It also fits naturally with my selling-by-helping methodology. You can connect directly with your ideal customers, and Advice Sessions let you offer one-on-one help right from your LinkedIn profile, so leading with value becomes part of how you do business.

Not all of your business will come through LinkedIn, but that’s one more reason to get your presence right. Whenever I help someone in a public forum, the next thing I do is connect with them on LinkedIn, always with a personalized note, so the relationship starts naturally. From there, I can stay in touch, and my ideal clients can see the content I create and share.

That content should lead with value, too. Teach, share what you’re learning and answer the questions your ideal clients are already asking. Then, when they’re ready for a transformation of their own, you’ll be the first person they think to call.

LinkedIn Premium Business can also help you get that content in front of more of your ideal clients, expanding your network and boosting your visibility, while embracing my selling-by-helping methodology at every touchpoint.

According to recent reports, if you’re ready to start selling by helping, LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to find the ones that fit how you work.

Industry observers note that by all accounts, I was a phenomenal salesperson. I always exceeded my quota, which in the sales world meant that my quota increased every year. But just because I was effective doesn’t mean that I loved it.

When you’re selling inside a large organization with a seven-figure quota, there are things you simply have to do to hit your numbers. For me, that meant pushing and pitching to just about anyone who would listen, and it took a heavy toll on my mental health.

The toll came from feeling that I had to do things that didn’t align with my ethics or my entrepreneurial beliefs. In the seven years I’ve run my agency, I haven’t had to compromise my ethics to build a book of business or grow my pipeline. Instead, I’ve focused on what I call selling by helping.

BTR sector fears Treasury rules move the goal line on investor ban

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.
  • Department of the Treasury‘s public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban.
  • BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into new projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn’t know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out.

Monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury‘s public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban. Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands.

BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into new projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.

According to recent reports, last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals.

Industry observers note that treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption.

Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, stated in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including:.

Recent findings suggest that these letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow.

Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed.

It has been revealed that the chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether.

That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project.

Sources indicate that richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences, argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell.

Industry observers note that “To build and stabilize a new community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross noted in an interview.

Sources indicate that the letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold.

It has been revealed that the letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects.

“A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read.

In a recent development, additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners’ ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry.

“If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and newly introduced construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read.

To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction.

Sources indicate that quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold.

Treasury’s proposed rulemaking describes the three activities that could qualify an institutional investor as a covered entity as “purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains”. This matters because BTR developers often build and retain homes as rental properties before selling stabilized communities to finance future developments.

Treasury’s language is ambiguous, leaving open the possibility that BTR developers could be treated like institutional investors.

It has been revealed that the National Rental Home Council made this a central argument in its letter, distinguishing between an investor buying a home from someone else and one acting as the builder. The organization urged Treasury to recognize that developers who build and retain homes as rentals operate differently from investors who purchase newly built homes from third parties.

Up for Growth Action made a similar argument, urging Treasury to differentiate between creating latest rental housing and acquiring existing housing.

Industry observers note that several letters argued that Treasury’s proposed rule does not clearly distinguish single-plat rental communities, where multiple homes share one parcel and common ownership, from individual single-family homes. They worry the rule could inadvertently restrict the development, ownership or sale of these communities by treating them as collections of individual homes subject to the institutional investor ban.

In response, BTR advocates argued for clearer rules for single-plat communities and those mixing renters and owners, while NRHC asked whether buildings with three or more attached units could count as single-family homes.

The letters also raise concerns about the proposed exception for investors that purchase distressed homes, substantially rehabilitate them and rent them out. Treasury’s proposed rules would allow institutional investors to purchase existing homes in need of extensive repairs, as long as they spend 15% of the purchase price on improvements.

However, several of the letters argued that the 15% threshold is too high. They further argued that the rule could be hard to enforce for homes that are difficult to inspect before purchase, homes in jurisdictions without applicable local codes, and homes with problems that aren’t obvious upfront.

Industry observers note that rental housing advocates disagreed on how flexible the rehabilitation threshold should be. While some groups advocated for increasing the threshold, NMHC, NAA and RETTC support the 15% benchmark while advocating for more flexibility in identifying problems and applying older building standards.

The common theme is that industry leaders want the exception to work for genuinely distressed properties without requiring investors to predict every hidden problem before purchasing a home.
